newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: No budget cut in Australia social security change.
newsitem.headline: No budget cut in Australia social security change.

text.p: Amendments to Australian social security announced this week will have no significant effect on the government's budget, a government spokesman said on Wednesday.

The streamlining of youth allowances, such as Austudy and unemployment benefits into a "common youth allowance", was not a budget measure, the spokesman for Social Security Minister Jocelyn Newman told Reuters.
"It's not a savings measure," he said.
He said although it was not detailed in the May 13 budget, the measure would cost about A$25 million to set up in the first year, 1998, and then go into being fairly neutral.

Social Security Minister Jocelyn Newman said on Tuesday that under the changes, five unemployment and education benefits would be combined into a single, parental means-tested common youth allowance, due to start in July, 1998.
Newman said the allowance -- which replaces Austudy for full-time students aged up to 25 and the dole for those aged up to 21 -- would encourage young people to study.
Under the new allowance unemployment benefits for 16 to 17-year-olds would be abolished and jobless 18 to 20-year-olds would be subject to a parental means test.
Rent assistance would also be extended to students who live away from home to study.
But Opposition Labor Leader Kim Beazley said the youth allowance would put a price tag on family values.
"The price tag is A$41,000," he said on Australian Broadcasting Corp radio. "If you're over that you bear the full burden yourself," he said.
Australian Democrats Social Security spokesman John Woodley said the allowance was anti-family and anti-young people.
"What this is going to do is put more pressure on families and we're going to see more teenage suicides," Woodley said on Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
